'''Tamás Székely''' (born 24 May 1959)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Wissenschaftskolleg zu Berlin |url=https://www.wiko-berlin.de/en/fellows/academic-year/2016/szekely-tamas |access-date=2023-12-20 |website=Tamás Székely, Dr. |language=en-US}}</ref> is a Hungarian [[Evolutionary biology|evolutionary biologist]] and [[Conservation biology|conservationist]]. He is the Professor of Biodiversity at the [[University of Bath]] and he holds an Honorary Professor position at the [[University of Debrecen]], Hungary. He is also the Director of the Debrecen Biodiversity Centre. His 1999 article, ''Brood Desertion in [[Kentish plover|Kentish Plover]]'',<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Szekely |first=T. |date=1999-03-01 |title=Brood desertion in Kentish plover: sex differences in remating opportunities |url=https://academic.oup.com/beheco/article-lookup/doi/10.1093/beheco/10.2.185 |journal=Behavioral Ecology |volume=10 |issue=2 |pages=185–190 |doi=10.1093/beheco/10.2.185|url-access=subscription }}</ref> examined sex differences in remating opportunities following brood desertion, demonstrating the social environment's influence on [[Parental care in birds|parental care]] dynamics.

His research focuses on Székely the demographic hypothesis regarding the origin of [[Reproduction|sex roles]]. In 2007, Székely co-edited ''Sex, Size & Gender Roles'',<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Székely |first1=Tamás |title=Social behaviour: genes, ecology and evolution |last2=Moore |first2=Allen Jonathan |last3=Komdeur |first3=Jan |date=2010 |publisher=Cambridge university press |isbn=978-0-521-88317-7 |location=New York}}</ref> confirming [[Charles Darwin|Darwin]]'s conjectures that [[sexual selection]] is a major contributor to the overall pattern of [[Sexual dimorphism|male-biased size dimorphism]] in [[mammal]]s, [[bird]]s, and [[reptile]]s. Alongside others, he identified that the distribution of size differences between sexes in birds and mammals is [[leptokurtic]]. Székely co-edited ''Social Behaviour''<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |url=https://academic.oup.com/book/12169 |title=Sex, Size and Gender Roles: Evolutionary Studies of Sexual Size Dimorphism |date=2007-07-05 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-170903-6 |language=en |doi=10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199208784.001.0001 |editor-last1=Fairbairn |editor-last2=Blanckenhorn |editor-last3=Székely |editor-first1=Daphne J. |editor-first2=Wolf U. |editor-first3=Tamás }}</ref> in 2010, offering an integrative perspective on studying [[Behavioral ecology|behavioral]] complexity. Alongside Allen J. Moore and Jan Komdeur, he coined the term ''systems biology approach''. Additionally, he founded the Maio Biodiversity Foundation in [[Cape Verde|Cabo Verde]] in 2010.

== Education ==
In 1978, Tamás Székely commenced his studies at Kossuth University (now the [[University of Debrecen]]), [[Hungary]], and successfully obtained a diploma in teaching [[biology]] and [[chemistry]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Székely |first=Tamás |title=Tamás Székely Curriculum Vitae & List of Publications |url=https://static1.squarespace.com/static/64faffb7df96b510ab232e39/t/6583155685963e36ed0f3685/1703089496068/T+Szekely_CV+%26+Publications+September+2023.pdf |access-date=20 December 2023 |website=szekelylab.com}}</ref> From 1983 to 1986, he dedicated himself to his Ph.D. training at Kossuth University, concentrating on the temporal patterns of [[Ecological niche|niche structure]] in forest [[passerine]] birds.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Magyar Királyi Madártani Intézet. |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/91405 |title=Aquila |last2=Intézet |first2=Magyar Királyi Madártani |last3=Intézet |first3=Magyar Madártani |last4=központ |first4=Magyar ornithologiai |date=1986 |publisher=A Magyar Ornithologiai Knt Kiadva |volume=v.93-94 (1986-1987) |location=Budapest}}</ref> The foundational conceptual framework he developed during these years was significantly shaped by Prof. Zoltán Varga's integrative research approach, emphasizing the critical importance of [[Phylogenetic tree|phylogeny]] in comprehending core patterns in [[ecology]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Székely |first=Tamás |date=2023-09-19 |title=Evolution of reproductive strategies: sex roles, sex ratios and phylogenies |journal=Biologia Futura |language=en |doi=10.1007/s42977-023-00177-0 |issn=2676-8607|doi-access=free }}</ref>

From 1987 to 1988, he spent a year as a postdoctoral research fellow at the [[Edward Grey Institute of Field Ornithology]] at [[Oxford]], where he delved into the emerging topic of [[Reproduction|reproductive strategies]] within the nascent field of [[sociobiology]] (known as [[behavioral ecology]] in Europe).<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />

== Work ==

=== Evolutionary Biology ===
Székely and his research team is recognized for describing the interactions of the components of [[Reproduction|sex roles]] in non-human animals: [[Mate choice|mate selection]], [[parental care]], and [[Pair bond|pair-bonding]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Székely |first1=Tamás |last2=Carmona‐Isunza |first2=Maria C. |last3=Engel |first3=Noémie |last4=Halimubieke |first4=Naerhulan |last5=Jones |first5=William |last6=Kubelka |first6=Vojtĕch |last7=Rice |first7=Romy |last8=Tanner |first8=Claire E. |last9=Tóth |first9=Zsófia |last10=Valdebenito |first10=José O. |last11=Wanders |first11=Kees |last12=McDonald |first12=Grant C. |date=2023-10-11 |title=The causes and implications of sex role diversity in shorebird breeding systems |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ibi.13277 |journal=Ibis |language=en |doi=10.1111/ibi.13277 |issn=0019-1019|doi-access=free }}</ref> His focus on [[Wader|shorebirds]], including [[plover]]s, [[sandpiper]]s, and related species, stems from the group's remarkable diversity in [[Mating system|breeding systems]], parenting behaviors, and [[Sexual dimorphism|sexual size dimorphism]].<ref name="Székely 923–933">{{Cite journal |last=Székely |first=Tamás |date=2019-07-01 |title=Why study plovers? The significance of non-model organisms in avian ecology, behaviour and evolution |journal=Journal of Ornithology |language=en |volume=160 |issue=3 |pages=923–933 |doi=10.1007/s10336-019-01669-4 |issn=2193-7206|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Using diverse methods including field studies,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Parra |first1=Jorge E. |last2=Beltrán |first2=Marcela |last3=Zefania |first3=Sama |last4=Dos Remedios |first4=Natalie |last5=Székely |first5=Tamás |date=2014-04-01 |title=Experimental assessment of mating opportunities in three shorebird species |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0003347214000050 |journal=Animal Behaviour |volume=90 |pages=83–90 |doi=10.1016/j.anbehav.2013.12.030 |s2cid=15727544 |issn=0003-3472|url-access=subscription }}</ref> comparative analysis,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Halimubieke |first1=Naerhulan |last2=Kupán |first2=Krisztina |last3=Valdebenito |first3=José O. |last4=Kubelka |first4=Vojtěch |last5=Carmona-Isunza |first5=María Cristina |last6=Burgas |first6=Daniel |last7=Catlin |first7=Daniel |last8=St Clair |first8=James J. H. |last9=Cohen |first9=Jonathan |last10=Figuerola |first10=Jordi |last11=Yasué |first11=Maï |last12=Johnson |first12=Matthew |last13=Mencarelli |first13=Mauro |last14=Cruz-López |first14=Medardo |last15=Stantial |first15=Michelle |date=2020-09-23 |title=Successful breeding predicts divorce in plovers |journal=Scientific Reports |language=en |volume=10 |issue=1 |page=15576 |doi=10.1038/s41598-020-72521-6  |doi-access=free|issn=2045-2322 |pmc=7511398 |pmid=32968190|bibcode=2020NatSR..1015576H }}</ref> and dynamic [[game theory]] modeling,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Barta |first1=Zoltán |last2=Székely |first2=Tamás |last3=Liker |first3=András |last4=Harrison |first4=Freya |date=June 2014 |title=Social Role Specialization Promotes Cooperation between Parents |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/676014 |journal=The American Naturalist |language=en |volume=183 |issue=6 |pages=747–761 |doi=10.1086/676014 |pmid=24823819 |issn=0003-0147|doi-access=free |hdl=2437/195642 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> he and his team has uncovered the influence of breeding systems, environmental conditions, and sexual dimorphism<ref name=":0" /> on [[Courtship display|courtship behaviors]] and sex biases.

His team also showed the crucial role of the social environment,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Végvári |first1=Zsolt |last2=Katona |first2=Gergely |last3=Vági |first3=Balázs |last4=Freckleton |first4=Robert P. |last5=Gaillard |first5=Jean‐Michel |last6=Székely |first6=Tamás |last7=Liker |first7=András |date=July 2018 |title=Sex‐biased breeding dispersal is predicted by social environment in birds |journal=Ecology and Evolution |language=en |volume=8 |issue=13 |pages=6483–6491 |doi=10.1002/ece3.4095  |doi-access=free|issn=2045-7758 |pmc=6053579 |pmid=30038750|bibcode=2018EcoEv...8.6483V }}</ref> particularly the [[Sex ratio|adult sex ratio]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Székely |first1=T. |last2=Weissing |first2=F. J. |last3=Komdeur |first3=J. |date=August 2014 |title=Adult sex ratio variation: implications for breeding system evolution |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jeb.12415 |journal=Journal of Evolutionary Biology |language=en |volume=27 |issue=8 |pages=1500–1512 |doi=10.1111/jeb.12415 |pmid=24848871 |issn=1010-061X|doi-access=free }}</ref> in predicting parental cooperation across taxa. Their research also discovered formerly unknown adaptive parental care strategies that influence individual reproductive success, like the fact that incubating parent birds serve as visual cues to [[Predation|predators]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Engel |first1=Noémie |last2=Végvári |first2=Zsolt |last3=Rice |first3=Romy |last4=Kubelka |first4=Vojtěch |last5=Székely |first5=Tamás |date=2020-07-29 |title=Incubating parents serve as visual cues to predators in Kentish plover (Charadrius alexandrinus) |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=15 |issue=7 |article-number=e0236489 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0236489 |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=7390395 |pmid=32726365 |bibcode=2020PLoSO..1536489E |doi-access=free }}</ref>

=== Conservation ===
Székely is renowned for both his theoretical and practical interventions in the conservation of shorebirds, [[water bird]]s,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rabenandrasana |first1=Marc |last2=Zefania |first2=Sama |last3=Long |first3=Peter |last4=Seing |first4=Sam The |last5=Virginie |first5=Marie Clémentine |last6=Randrianarisoa |first6=Mihaja |last7=Safford |first7=Roger |last8=Székely |first8=Tama´s |date=March 2009 |title=Distribution, habitat and status of 'Endangered' Sakalava Rail of Madagascar |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/bird-conservation-international/article/distribution-habitat-and-status-of-endangered-sakalava-rail-of-madagascar/2C99330DE1BB58219905B4CA2ED590E9 |journal=Bird Conservation International |language=en |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=23–32 |doi=10.1017/S0959270908008058 |issn=1474-0001|doi-access=free }}</ref> and marine [[fauna]], including [[shark]]s, [[whale]]s, and [[sea turtle]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lopes |first1=Katia |last2=Passos |first2=Leno |last3=Rodrigues |first3=João Garcia |last4=Koenen |first4=Franziska |last5=Stiebens |first5=Victor |last6=Székely |first6=Tamás |last7=Dutra |first7=Amanda |date=December 2016 |title=Sea Turtle, Shark, and Dolphin Bycatch Rates by Artisanal and Semi-Industrial Fishers in Maio Island, Cape Verde |url=https://bioone.org/journals/chelonian-conservation-and-biology/volume-15/issue-2/CB-1213.1/Sea-Turtle-Shark-and-Dolphin-Bycatch-Rates-by-Artisanal-and/10.2744/CB-1213.1.full |journal=Chelonian Conservation and Biology |volume=15 |issue=2 |pages=279–288 |doi=10.2744/CB-1213.1 |s2cid=89848870 |issn=1071-8443|doi-access=free }}</ref>

In 2010, Székely founded the Maio Biodiversity Foundation (FMB, as per its Portuguese acronym) in [[Cape Verde|Cabo Verde]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Letter: Cape Verde is biodiversity template for West Africa |url=https://www.ft.com/content/f3f77f22-e373-451f-b5c2-7008114bd05b |access-date=2023-12-20 |website=www.ft.com}}</ref> The foundation's mission is to protect wildlife and natural habitats by actively engaging with local communities, with a focus on safeguarding sharks, whales, sea turtles, and various bird species.<ref name="Admin">{{Cite web |last=Admin |date=2020-06-10 |title=Sea Guardians Protecting Cape Verde's Marine Life |url=https://www.maiocapeverde.com/latest/sea-guardians-protecting-cape-verdes-marine-life.html |access-date=2023-12-20 |website=Maio Cape Verde |language=en-GB}}</ref> The conservation initiatives by FMB played a pivotal role in the designation of Salina Porto Ingles, one of Cape Verde's key shorebird breeding sites, as a [[Ramsar Convention|Ramsar]] Site.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cape Verde designates salt flats for Ramsar List {{!}} The Convention on Wetlands, The Convention on Wetlands |url=https://www.ramsar.org/news/cape-verde-designates-salt-flats-ramsar-list |access-date=2023-12-20 |website=www.ramsar.org |language=en}}</ref>

=== Achievements ===
Throughout his career, Prof Székely's research has not only been recognised through awards, but his contributions to the field has improved our knowledge and understanding of the field of social behaviour.
In 2010, Prof Szekely founded the FMB (Maio Biodiversity Foundation)<ref name="Admin"/> conservation NGO in Cape Verde and lead the NGO as its president for 8 years. 
Prof Székely developed both a field methodology and research protocol for investigating shorebird social behaviour, which is now widely used around the globe [Szekely & Kosztolanyi 2006,.<ref name="Székely 923–933"/><ref name="doi.org"/> Through the use of this protocol, he analysed mathematically, experimentally and phylogenetically reproductive strategies. More recently, this has progressed into having developed a general framework for understanding the causes and consequences of adult sex ratio variation for social evolution.
In addition, he identified sexual selection as a major driver of the Rensch's rule.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Székely |first=Tamás |last2=Freckleton |first2=Robert P. |last3=Reynolds |first3=John D. |date=August 2004 |title=Sexual selection explains Rensch's rule of size dimorphism in shorebirds |journal=PNAS |volume=37 |issue=101 |pages=12224–12227 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0404503101 |hdl=10261/43254 |hdl-access=free |pmc=514460 }}</ref>

=== Media ===
In 2020, Prof Szekely was recognised for his work on social behaviour by being interviewed for the "Staff Spotlight" (https://www.bath.ac.uk/announcements/staff-spotlight-on-tamas-szekely/ ).
In addition, Prof Szekely's research has been in numerous news articles, such as the BBC "Sex role reversal: Female shorebirds rule the roost" (https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/science-environment-21741912 ), Audubon "The Arctic is no longer a safe haven for breeding shorebirds" (an American magazine (https://www.audubon.org/news/the-arctic-no-longer-safe-haven-breeding-shorebirds), Science News "Climate change may have made the Arctic deadlier for baby shorebirds" (https://www.sciencenews.org/article/climate-change-may-have-made-arctic-deadlier-baby-shorebirds), Science Daily "Decline in shorebirds linked to climate change, experts warn" (https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2018/11/181108142405.htm)  and EukekAlert! "Decline in shorebirds linked to climate change, experts warn" (https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/600065).
